About: Faraday's Magnet & Coil

Source

Concept
Electromagnetic induction — only a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an EMF (Faraday's law, ε = −N dΦ/dt).
Serves
The full causal chain: moving magnet → changing flux → EMF → current → light. Brightness tracks I², so faster motion, more loops, or larger loop area all brighten the bulb for the same reason: bigger dΦ/dt.
Inquiry
Static vs moving magnet: why does a magnet held still — however strong — leave the bulb dark, while the same magnet in motion lights it?
Misconception
That a magnet near a coil makes current — i.e. that a stationary magnet induces current. It cannot: constant flux means dΦ/dt = 0, so ε = 0 and I = 0.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The apparatus

A bar magnet lies on the axis of a coil of N loops whose ends are joined through a bulb. The magnetic flux through one loop is Φ = B·A·cos θ; on the axis θ = 0, so each loop links B·A and the whole coil links N·B·A.

2 · A magnet at rest

The magnet is slid up against the coil and then held there, motionless. While it is held there, the bulb:

3 · Motion against rest

Move the magnet in to the coil, hold it, then pull it out. Compare the bulb during the motion with the bulb at rest, and the sign of ε going in with the sign coming out.

4 · The same sweep, four times faster

The same in-and-out sweep is repeated in one quarter of the time. Compared with the slow sweep, the peak induced EMF is:

5 · Rewinding the coil

The magnet now oscillates on the axis: the flux rises and falls repeatedly and the current reverses each half cycle — an AC generator. Rewound from 1 loop to 4, same motion, the induced EMF is:

The Physics

Faraday’s Magnet & Coil · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A bar magnet moves along the axis of a coil of N loops, and the coil's ends are joined through a bulb. The sim reads out the flux linkage Φ, the induced EMF ε, the current I and the bulb's brightness, all in relative units.

What you'll learn

  • What flux linkage is, and what sets its size.
  • How the flux, the EMF and the current are linked.
  • How the number of loops, the loop area and the magnet's strength matter.
  • What the bulb's brightness does and does not tell you.
The apparatus: a bar magnet and a coil on one axis, wired to a bulb.

What's on screen

  • Bar magnet, S on the left and N on the right. Drag it along the axis.
  • Coil of one to four loops, with the bulb above it. You can drag the coil too.
  • Field arrows, fainter where B is weaker, and electrons drifting round the loops.
See itStart from the opening state, with the magnet swinging back and forth. Watch for: the magnet moving along the axis while the flux, EMF and current readouts keep changing.

The sim opens playing. Drag the magnet and the swing pauses while you hold it, and drag the coil to move it past a still magnet. Values marked * are relative units, with the circuit resistance R = 1.

03

Flux linkage is N times B times A

The magnetic flux through one loop is Φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between the field and the loop's normal. The magnet sits on the coil's axis, so θ = 0 and one loop links BA.

Φ = N B A
The sim's flux linkage readout: N loops in series, each linking the same BA.

B is the magnet's field at the coil. It is greatest when the magnet is centred in the coil and drops steeply with distance. A is the loop area. At the opening settings the magnet is parked away from the coil and the readout shows Φ = 0.094 Wb*. Slide the magnet into the coil, with its centre in the coil's plane, and it reads 0.750 Wb*.

Raising N, A or the magnet's strength raises Φ in proportion. At full strength, with N = 4 loops and A = 100%, a magnet centred in the coil gives Φ = 4.000 Wb*.

See itSet the strength to 100%, N = 4 and the area to 100%, then hold the magnet centred in the coil. Watch for: the flux linkage reading 4.000 Wb*.
04

Only a changing flux induces an EMF

Faraday's law says the induced EMF depends on how fast the flux changes, not on how big it is:

ε = −N dΦ1/dt = −dΦ/dt
Φ1 = BA is one loop's flux and Φ = NBA is the readout.

A magnet held still gives a constant flux. Then dΦ/dt = 0, so ε = 0, I = ε/R = 0 and the bulb is dark. This holds however strong the magnet is and however close it sits.

Move the magnet and Φ changes, so ε and I appear. The sim computes ε every frame from the change in Φ, so a held magnet really does read +0.000 V*. Hand-moving the coil past a still magnet works the same way: only the relative motion changes the flux.

See itPause with the magnet held centred in the coil at full strength. Watch for: Φ at 1.000 Wb*, ε and I both at 0.000, and the bulb dark.
05

Faster motion means a larger EMF

The same change in Φ squeezed into a shorter time is a greater rate dΦ/dt. Do the same sweep in one quarter of the time and dΦ/dt, and with it ε, is four times larger. Doubling the speed doubles ε.

In the sim the magnet swings back and forth at the Oscillation speed. At the opening 0.50 Hz the largest EMF reading is about 0.5 V*, and at 1.0 Hz it is about 1.0 V*. At 1.5 Hz it reaches about 1.5 V*.

The sim smooths ε with a very short lag of 0.02 s, so the readings come out a little under the ideal proportion. Look for a clear doubling, not an exact one. The speed button changes only how fast the clock runs on screen, not the physics.

See itSet the oscillation speed to 1.00 Hz and watch the EMF reading. Watch for: ε swinging up to about 1.0 V* either way, about double the opening swing.
06

Turns, area and strength scale the EMF

The N loops are wired in series, so their EMFs add. Every loop links the same changing flux BA, and the coil delivers N times one loop's EMF. The flux is not shared out between the loops.

A larger loop links more of the field, so the EMF grows in proportion to A. A stronger magnet raises B everywhere, so ε grows in proportion to the strength too. All three scale the EMF for the same motion.

At the opening 0.50 Hz swing the peak ε is about 0.26 V* with one loop and about 1.05 V* with four. With two loops it is about 0.53 V*. Area at 20% gives about 0.21 V* and at 100% about 1.05 V*.

See itSet N = 4 and let the magnet swing. Watch for: ε peaking near 1.05 V*, twice the opening swing of about 0.53 V*.
See itSet the loop area to 100% and let the magnet swing. Watch for: ε peaking near 1.05 V* again, with the loops drawn larger.
07

The sign of ε flips with the direction of motion

The minus sign in Faraday's law is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux that causes it. A magnet moving toward the coil makes Φ grow, so ε is negative in the sim. A magnet moving away makes Φ shrink, so ε is positive.

The electrons show it. They drift round the loops one way while the magnet approaches and the other way while it leaves. ε also drops to a small value at the ends of each swing, where the magnet stops for an instant and Φ stops changing.

A magnet swinging steadily therefore drives a current that reverses every half cycle. That is an AC generator, and the same idea turns the motion of coils and magnets in a power station into mains electricity.

See itStart from the opening state and watch the ε readout through one swing. Watch for: ε negative while the magnet moves toward the coil and positive while it moves away, with the electrons reversing.
08

Brightness follows I²

Ohm's law gives the current, I = ε/R, and the bulb's power is P = I²R. The sim sets R = 1, so I has the same value as ε, and the brightness follows I².

Doubling ε doubles I and quadruples the brightness. The bulb cannot tell the sign of the current, so it glows for both directions of motion. At the opening swing the peak current is about 0.53 A*, so the bulb peaks at about 56%.

The bulb is fully lit once |I| reaches 0.70 A*, and the readout then says 100% · maxed. From there, ε and I keep growing while the bulb stays put. Compare circuits by their ε and I readouts, not by how bright the bulb looks.

See itSet N = 4 and let the magnet swing. Watch for: the bulb reading 100% · maxed at the peaks while ε is still about 1.05 V*.
09

Summary

In one line. A magnet on a coil's axis gives the coil a flux linkage Φ = NBA, and the bulb on the coil reports the EMF that results.

Key points

  • Flux linkage Φ = NBA. B is strongest next to the magnet and falls steeply with distance.
  • ε = −dΦ/dt, so only a changing flux gives ε. The minus sign is Lenz's law and flips with the direction of motion.
  • For the same motion, ε grows with the speed, the number of loops, the loop area and the magnet's strength.
  • I = ε/R and the bulb follows I², until it pins at 100%.

Common mix-ups

  • "A strong magnet near a coil makes a current." Strength raises Φ but not dΦ/dt, so a still magnet gives none.
  • "A brighter bulb always means a bigger ε." The bulb maxes out at |I| = 0.70 A*, but ε keeps growing.

Things to try on your own

  • Drag the coil past the held magnet and watch ε appear.
  • Set the strength to 0% and swing the magnet.
  • Turn the field arrows off and find where in the swing ε is at its largest.
